Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never alone with another person' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The triggers, threat items, and memory content suggest a combat/military trauma pattern centered on environmental danger cues (fire, silence, shouting, sensory flashback phenomena), not an interpersonal danger pattern specifically involving being alone with another person. This strategy therefore appears to address a different trauma context than the one represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual or severe interpersonal violation trauma. In this profile, the surrounding triggers, memory, and threat items point to a military combat-type danger formulation rather than contamination-based shame. Paired with the 'never alone with another person' strategy, it pulls the profile toward a different trauma meaning structure that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: Elena, fifty-four, spent twenty-two years as a combat engineer, her hands accustomed to stabilizing collapsed terrain and routing explosive hazards. That professional certainty shattered in a narrow desert pass when a concealed charge detonated ahead of her convoy. The lead vehicle erupted into a rolling fireball, and Elena felt the searing heat of the blast imprint on her forearms before the desert night rushed in, dropping the temperature sharply against her sweat-soaked uniform. As she scrambled toward a rocky overhang, the radio cracked with frantic shouting, drowning out all coherent commands. In that moment, her mind refused to stitch the event into a linear sequence; she could not tell a clear story of what happened even to herself, only a fractured collage of smoke, blistering heat, and fractured voices. Years later, that specific sequence of sensory violations continued to dictate her reality. Whenever she encountered roaring campfires, sudden drafts of cold air, or raised voices in her civilian architecture firm, her autonomic nervous system immediately flooded her with physiological alarms. These cues did not merely alert her; they bypassed conscious processing and instantly dragged her back to the pass, replaying the radio chatter and the scent of burning rubber in her mind. The relentless repetition of these sensory spikes convinced her that the world was a dangerously unpredictable place and that the injustice of her survival remained entirely unaddressed. Her conviction that she was fundamentally broken and that the environment was hostile kept her body on perpetual alert, while her expectation of danger sharpened her attention, causing ordinary stimuli to immediately trigger the same physiological cascade. Because the memories arrived without warning, carrying the visceral weight of the original terror, Elena began constantly scanning every client meeting room for sightlines and exits. The unprocessed flashbacks kept her physiological arousal locked in a heightened state of readiness, deepening her sense of injustice and reinforcing her belief that there was something wrong with her as a person. Unable to tolerate the exhausting tension or the difficulty concentrating on structural load-bearing calculations, Elena began avoiding anything that could be stressful. She stopped attending industry conferences, retreated into emotional numbing when her husband Mateo tried to discuss their strained marriage, and developed a rigid habit of checking every exit. This avoidance and hyper-vigilance, however, quickly curdled back into self-condemnation; she interpreted her withdrawal as moral failure. The more she checked her surroundings and numbed her emotions, the more she isolated herself from normalizing feedback, ensuring that minor temperature shifts or distant echoes immediately sparked fresh waves of threat monitoring. Maintaining this rigid routine exhausted her, ensuring her body remained locked in alert mode rather than recovering from the past, guaranteeing that the memories would continue to intrude, the appraisals would harden, and the cycle would tighten until the mounting isolation finally drove her to a veteran clinic. Her PCL-5 score of 62 confirmed what she had lived with for months. She sat in the intake room now, fearing that if she did not find a way to quiet the constant readiness, she would lose the last vestiges of the marriage she had fought so hard to protect, desperate for a path back to the stability she believed she had irreparably lost.
